narrativeReportMd:
# AppointmentResponse R4→R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
No local R4-valid `AppointmentResponse` instance pattern was found that becomes invalid solely because of a required field removal or cardinality tightening in R6. The material risks are mostly R6→R4 representability and runtime/codegen risks: R6 adds `entered-in-error` to the required participant status binding, permits `Group` actors, changes `comment` from `string` to `markdown`, and adds explicit counter-proposal and recurrence fields.

## Scope
The comparison used the supplied R4 and R6 core package StructureDefinitions and related local ValueSets/CodeSystems. Inherited `Resource`, `DomainResource`, `Element`, and primitive-base changes are excluded from findings and noted as out of scope.

## Main migration themes
R6 makes several formerly implicit scheduling concepts explicit. `proposedNewTime` distinguishes counter-proposals from ordinary confirmations that happen to repeat start/end times, and recurrence fields identify whether a response applies to all occurrences or a specific occurrence. R6 also broadens participants by allowing `Group` as `actor` and makes the status lifecycle safer by adding `entered-in-error` as a required-code option.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact local issue is `participantStatus`: R6-valid `entered-in-error` cannot be represented as a valid R4 participant status and is clinically/business significant because the element is a modifier. The recurrence additions are also high-impact for down-conversion because dropping them can change whether a response applies to one occurrence or all occurrences.

## Findings requiring human review
The `participantType` binding changed composition while remaining extensible. Without authoritative expansions for both terminology versions, removed versus added code coverage is only partly computable from the supplied package files.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Most changes were made as additive optional elements or widened domains, which avoids direct R4→R6 validation breaks. The less-compatible parts are a required binding value-set replacement for status, a reference target widening, and a primitive type replacement that can affect generated APIs and rendering.

## Follow-up analysis
Analyze `Appointment` alongside this report for recurrence and participant matching behavior, and perform official terminology expansions for `encounter-participant-type` before final migration rules are locked down.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: No hard local R4→R6 validation break was found for existing `AppointmentResponse` elements. The top migration concerns are the R6-only `entered-in-error` status, R6-only recurrence/counter-proposal fields, `Group` actors, and codegen/rendering changes from `comment: string` to `comment: markdown`. The main uncertainty is exact `participantType` terminology expansion impact.
summary.migrationThemesMd: R4→R6 migration should preserve all existing common fields, then enrich records where possible: derive `proposedNewTime` from business context when start/end differ from the referenced Appointment, map recurrence intent into the new recurrence fields when known, and update status enums to include `entered-in-error`. R6→R4 conversion needs explicit loss handling for `entered-in-error`, `Group` actors, and recurrence-specific fields because R4 has no native slots for them.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural deltas because both assigned StructureDefinitions are present and have the same canonical identity. Confidence is high for `participantStatus` because local ValueSets and CodeSystems show the added code. Confidence is medium for `participantType` because the R6 value set references external terminology package versions whose full expansions were not available in the supplied core package.

semanticText.comment: This element is labeled as a modifier because the status contains the code entered-in-error that marks the participant as not currently valid.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 keeps the field mandatory and modifier, but makes `entered-in-error` a valid required-binding code and clarifies the modifier reason.

facts.note: R6-valid instances can now explicitly mark the AppointmentResponse as entered in error.

facts.oldValue: Not known why this is labelled a modifier
facts.newValue: This element is labelled as a modifier because it is a status element that contains status entered-in-error which means that the resource should not be treated as valid

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element id and path are unchanged; only the required binding target, code coverage, short text, and modifier reason changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Existing R4 status codes remain valid in R6, so this is not an R4→R6 validation break. It is high impact for R6→R4 and runtime handling because `participantStatus` is a required modifier element: an R6 instance with `entered-in-error` cannot satisfy R4's required value set, and systems that ignore the new code may treat an invalidated response as clinically or operationally active.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Misinterpreting `entered-in-error` can cause a scheduling response that should be disregarded to be acted on.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow AppointmentResponse to be explicitly invalidated using the common appointment lifecycle status.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: R6 retains all R4 participantStatus codes and only adds entered-in-error.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal is reasonable: AppointmentResponse needed a standard way to mark a response as entered in error, and the R4 element text already hinted at that modifier meaning even though the R4 value set lacked the code. Because R6 preserves the old required codes, this is not a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design issue; the material breakage is for R6-to-R4 conversion and systems with closed status enums.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: An R4 extension or conversion policy for `entered-in-error` is a mitigation, not a less-breaking R6 base design. Keeping the new invalidation state outside the base required status would preserve more R6-to-R4 compatibility but would make a safety-relevant modifier state less discoverable and less uniformly handled. Since all R4 codes remain valid in R6, `backwardCompatibleAlternativeAvailable` is best classified as `Not applicable`.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No R4-valid status is rejected; the remaining costs are closed-enum/runtime handling and lossy R6-to-R4 conversion for the new modifier code.

evidence.detail: R4 binding is required to ValueSet/participationstatus|4.0.1.
R6 binding is required to ValueSet/appointmentresponse-status|6.0.0-ballot4.
R6 includes all participationstatus codes and adds appointmentstatus#entered-in-error.
The added code means the instance should not have been part of the patient's record.
evidence.quote: This instance should not have been part of this patient's medical record.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example is illustrative only. A real R6→R4 transform needs a policy because mapping `entered-in-error` to any R4 allowed code changes the resource meaning.

findings.narrativeMd: `AppointmentResponse.participantStatus` changed from a required binding to `participationstatus` to a new required value set that also permits `entered-in-error`. The element was already a modifier in R4, but R6 makes the modifier rationale operational by adding the missing status code. This is especially important for enum-based SDKs and business rules that switch over status values.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances using `accepted`, `declined`, `tentative`, or `needs-action` remain valid against the R6 required binding. An R6 instance using `entered-in-error` is not valid against R4's required value set. Strict R4 validators and generated R4 enums will reject or fail to parse the new code unless they preserve unknown codes out of band.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: R4→R6 code should add `entered-in-error` to generated status enums and ensure modifier-aware logic treats such responses as not valid for scheduling decisions. R6→R4 conversion should not silently coerce `entered-in-error` to another R4 status; preserve it in an extension, quarantine the instance, or require manual review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A backward-compatible design could have represented `entered-in-error` as an extension while keeping the R4 value set unchanged, but that would undercut the safety value of a required modifier status. The base terminology change is disruptive for R6→R4 but probably justified because it standardizes an already-described invalidation state.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `participantStatus` still accepts every R4 status code, but R6 adds `entered-in-error` to a required modifier status. That creates real work for closed status enums, status-switch business rules, and R6-to-R4 conversion, because the new invalidation state cannot be represented in R4's required value set without policy. The design is still proportionate: it standardizes a safety-relevant state on the status element rather than hiding it elsewhere.
keyEvidence: R4 `AppointmentResponse.participantStatus` is 1..1 `code`, modifier=true, required to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/participationstatus|4.0.1`, with short text `accepted | declined | tentative | needs-action`.

R6 keeps the same path/cardinality/type/modifier flag but binds required to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/appointmentresponse-status|6.0.0-ballot4`, whose compose includes all `participationstatus` codes plus `appointmentstatus#entered-in-error`.
R6 `CodeSystem-appointmentstatus` defines `entered-in-error` as an instance that should not have been part of the patient's medical record.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 AppointmentResponse is FMM 3 and trial-use, so compatibility has meaningful weight, especially for a required modifier status. That raises the bar above experimental content, but it does not outweigh a proportionate additive status that preserves all R4 codes.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen and R6-to-R4 loss: old R4 instances remain valid in R6, but generated status enums and scheduling logic must handle a new modifier code, and R6 instances using it are not valid against R4's required binding.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No compelling less-breaking R6 base design exists. Keeping the R4 value set would omit the invalidation state, and representing it only as an extension would make a modifier/safety status less visible to generic clients. Because all R4 codes remain valid, the main alternatives are mitigations for R6-to-R4 conversion rather than better base R6 designs.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: I agree with the existing report that this is not an R4-to-R6 instance break and that no less-breaking base alternative is needed, but the direct R4-to-R6 impact is lower than the reported High score suggests.

findings.title: actor reference target widened to allow Group

oldState.summary: Optional Reference limited to Patient, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, RelatedPerson, Device, HealthcareService, or Location.

semanticText.definition: A Person, Location, HealthcareService, or Device that is participating in the appointment.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could identify a single patient/person/practitioner role, device, service, or location as the responding actor, but not a `Group`.

newState.summary: Optional Reference adds Group to the allowed target profiles.

semanticText.definition: A Person, Location, HealthcareService, or Device that is participating in the appointment.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 can represent a group actor, such as a patient group or cohort, as the participant responding to an appointment request.

facts.note: All R4 target profiles are retained.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element id and path are unchanged and the target profile list is identical except for the added `Group` target.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The target widening is not an R4→R6 validation break because all R4 targets remain allowed. R6 instances that use `actor.reference = Group/...` are not conformant to the R4 target profile set, and generated clients with closed reference unions may need code changes.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Losing the fact that a response came from or applies to a group can change appointment participation semantics.

justification.inferredGoal: Support appointment responses involving groups of participants.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: adding Group is a target-domain widening that keeps every R4 actor target.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Supporting group participation in scheduling responses is a plausible R6 goal, and the base change was made by widening the target list rather than replacing old targets. That preserves R4-valid instances, so the issue is not a less-breaking R4-to-R6 design question, even though R6 `Group` actors need explicit handling by R4 converters and generated clients.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Using an extension for group actors would be a backport or down-conversion mitigation rather than a backward-compatible R6 base alternative. The R6 base design already keeps the old target profiles, and native `Group` support gives generic clients a computable target that an extension-only approach would not.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No R4 actor reference becomes invalid; the tradeoff is R6-to-R4 loss and codegen/runtime updates for clients with closed reference-target unions.

evidence.detail: R4 target profiles do not include Group.
R6 target profiles include Group in addition to the R4 targets.

examples.examplesMd: The example is valid only for the target-domain point; a full instance would also need the referenced resources and any applicable scheduling context.

findings.narrativeMd: `AppointmentResponse.actor` now permits a `Group` reference. This is additive for R6 but matters to generated code because many SDKs model reference targets as closed unions or typed accessors.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4→R6 instances continue to validate if they used any of the old target profiles. R6→R4 instances with `Group` actors cannot be represented as R4-conformant `actor` references without either choosing individual members, using an extension, or relaxing validation.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update generated reference target lists and switch statements to include `Group`. For R6→R4 conversion, decide whether group actors should be expanded into multiple individual responses, retained as an extension, or rejected for manual handling; expansion is not always lossless.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Adding `Group` as a native target is a straightforward model widening. The less disruptive alternative would be an extension, but that would prevent generic scheduling clients from recognizing group participation.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `actor` is a straightforward target-list widening: R6 adds `Group` and retains every R4 target. R4 AppointmentResponse instances continue to validate, and the new target only affects systems that choose to consume R6 data with group actors or down-convert it to R4. That is normal model growth rather than a compatibility problem that needs standards redesign.
keyEvidence: R4 `AppointmentResponse.actor` target profiles are Patient, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, RelatedPerson, Device, HealthcareService, and Location.
R6 `AppointmentResponse.actor` adds `http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/Group` while retaining the R4 target profiles.
The element remains optional 0..1 Reference and summary=true in both versions.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 3/trial-use means target-list changes should still be checked, but the widening preserves R4-valid content and does not create enough stability pressure for a revisit.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: a new R6 `Group` actor has no conformant R4 target, and closed generated reference unions may need to recognize the new case; there is no old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 mechanism.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No less-breaking R6 base design is needed. An extension-only group actor would be less visible and less computable for generic R6 scheduling clients while preserving little beyond R4 down-conversion convenience.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: I agree with the evidence and the Not applicable alternative assessment, but I would not carry the existing Medium impact through to the final judgment because the base change is additive.

findings.title: comment type changed from string to markdown

semanticText.comment: This comment is particularly important when the responder is declining, tentatively accepting or requesting another time to indicate the reasons why.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 treated comments as plain string content.

semanticText.comment: This comment is particularly important when the responder is declining, tentatively accepting or requesting another time to indicate the reasons why.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 allows GitHub Flavored Markdown syntax in the same JSON property.

facts.note: The wire shape is unchanged, but the FHIR primitive type and generated API type can change.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element id and path are unchanged, with only the primitive type replaced.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The JSON scalar representation remains a string and `markdown` is a specialization of `string`, so ordinary R4 comment values should not become invalid merely because of this change. The main risks are generated-code type changes, validators that distinguish primitive types, and UI renderers that start interpreting formatting or links.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Comments can contain scheduling reasons. Rendering plain text as markdown without sanitization or review can alter displayed meaning or introduce unsafe links.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow richer explanatory text for declined, tentative, or counter-proposed appointment responses.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `comment` as `string` with clearer prose allowing Markdown, or add a parallel markdown comment while deprecating the old string field.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal of supporting richer human-facing explanatory text is reasonable, and `markdown` is still represented as a JSON string. The breakage is therefore mostly codegen, validator, and display-policy churn rather than ordinary instance invalidation. A less-breaking base design exists, but it would either fail to advertise Markdown intent computably or introduce duplicate comment fields for the same information.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The least disruptive base design would have left `AppointmentResponse.comment` as `string` and updated the definition to say Markdown syntax may be used when both systems agree. That preserves R4 wire shape and generated APIs but gives generic clients no reliable primitive-type signal for Markdown rendering or sanitization. A second `commentMarkdown`-style element would provide the signal but risks conflicting values and indefinite support for two same-resource representations.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Keeping only `string` loses a computable Markdown rendering signal; adding a parallel same-resource field creates duplicate comment representations that may conflict or never disappear.

evidence.detail: R4 type is `string`.
R6 type is `markdown`.
The markdown primitive is a string that may contain GitHub Flavored Markdown syntax.

migrationExampleJson.comment: Can attend if the visit starts after **10:00**.

examples.examplesMd: The same JSON member remains a string, but an R6 renderer may apply Markdown emphasis while an R4 renderer likely treated the value as plain text.

findings.narrativeMd: `AppointmentResponse.comment` changed primitive type from `string` to `markdown`. This is not a wire-format change, but it is a semantic and generated-model change: clients may now treat the content as renderable Markdown.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4-valid non-empty string should generally be acceptable as R6 markdown based on the primitive definitions inspected. R6 markdown can be placed in an R4 string field structurally, but the information that it was intended as Markdown is lost and R4 clients may display markup literally.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Regenerate models and update serializers, validators, and UI rendering policy for `comment`. Display code should sanitize Markdown output and tests should cover comments containing asterisks, links, line breaks, and plain text.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change could have been avoided by leaving `comment` as `string` because Markdown text can still be carried as ordinary text. The R6 choice makes rendering intent explicit at the cost of API churn.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `comment` changes from `string` to `markdown` on the same JSON property. Ordinary wire data remains a JSON string, and R6 markdown is defined as a string-derived primitive, so this is not a typical instance rejection. The real burden is generated API/type churn and display policy: clients may now need to treat the content as markdown, including rendering and sanitization choices.
keyEvidence: R4 `AppointmentResponse.comment` is optional 0..1 `string` with the same definition/comment text as R6.
R6 `StructureDefinition-markdown` has baseDefinition `http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/string` and describes markdown as a string that may contain GitHub Flavored Markdown syntax.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 3/trial-use makes an API-visible primitive type change worth taking seriously, but the unchanged scalar wire shape and reasonable richer-text goal keep this below Revisit.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen: generated models, validators that distinguish primitive types, and renderers may change behavior; old R4 string values should generally remain representable because the JSON shape is still a string.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A partial less-breaking design exists: keep `comment` as `string` and clarify that markdown may be used by agreement, or add a parallel markdown element. The first loses a computable rendering signal, and the second creates duplicate comment fields with possible conflicts, so the R6 choice is defensible.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree: the existing Medium impact and Partial alternative judgment match the fresh assessment, with the main risk in generated APIs and rendering semantics rather than hard validation.

findings.title: proposedNewTime added to explicitly mark counter-proposals

oldState.summary: No local element existed to explicitly indicate that start/end are a counter-proposed time.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 relied on `participantStatus` plus `start`/`end` differences from the referenced Appointment to imply a requested time change.

newState.summary: Optional boolean `proposedNewTime` was added with cardinality 0..1 and summary=true.

semanticText.definition: Indicates that the response is proposing a different time that was initially requested.  The new proposed time will be indicated in the start and end properties.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 can explicitly distinguish a response that proposes a new time from one that merely echoes the appointment time.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element has no R4 path and is a new local child in the R6 differential and snapshot.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The element is optional, so old R4 instances remain structurally valid after migration. The risk is semantic: R4 data may have implicit counter-proposals encoded only by differing `start`/`end`, while R6 systems may look for `proposedNewTime`; conversely R6 data with `proposedNewTime=true` loses that explicit flag in R4.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: A counter-proposed time can alter scheduling workflow and participant commitments.

justification.inferredGoal: Make counter-proposal semantics computable instead of implicit in start/end comparisons.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: `proposedNewTime` is optional additive R6 content and existing R4 instances can omit it.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal is to make counter-proposal semantics computable instead of relying on consumers to compare `start` and `end` with the referenced Appointment. Adding an optional boolean is a backward-safe base change for R4-to-R6 validation and a reasonable way to reduce ambiguity for R6 clients.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R4 extensions or business-rule inference can mitigate cross-version exchange, but they are not less-breaking R6 base designs. Keeping only the R4 implicit start/end comparison would avoid a new field but would not meet the R6 goal of making the counter-proposal flag explicit for generic clients.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The cost is semantic inference for migrated R4 data and lossy R6-to-R4 conversion, not rejection of R4-valid instances by the R6 base resource.

evidence.detail: No `AppointmentResponse.proposedNewTime` element exists in R4.
R6 adds optional boolean `proposedNewTime`.
evidence.quote: Indicates that the response is proposing a different time that was initially requested.

examples.examplesMd: R4 can carry the `start` and `end`, but not the explicit `proposedNewTime` flag.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds `proposedNewTime` so a responder can explicitly say that the included `start` and `end` are a counter-proposal. This converts an implicit comparison-based interpretation into a computable element.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances do not become invalid because the element is optional. R6 instances that use the element cannot be losslessly represented in R4 without an extension or inference from start/end values.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: When migrating R4 data, derive `proposedNewTime` only when the referenced Appointment is available and business rules confirm that `start`/`end` represent a counter-proposal. Do not set it solely because times are present; R4 also allowed times to confirm the existing appointment.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: An extension would have been less disruptive for R4 systems but less useful for generic R6 scheduling clients. Adding an optional boolean is a relatively backward-safe core change.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `proposedNewTime` is an optional additive boolean that makes an existing counter-proposal concept explicit. R4 instances can omit it, and the `start`/`end` definitions remain unchanged in R6, so migrated R4 data does not become structurally invalid. R6-to-R4 conversion may lose an explicit flag, but R4 already carried counter-proposal meaning through the timing fields.
keyEvidence: No `AppointmentResponse.proposedNewTime` element exists in the R4 StructureDefinition.
R6 adds `AppointmentResponse.proposedNewTime` as optional 0..1 `boolean`, summary=true, defined as indicating that the response proposes a different time.
R4 and R6 `AppointmentResponse.start` and `AppointmentResponse.end` retain the same timing/counter-proposal definitions.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 3/trial-use calls for checking semantic migration effects, but an optional additive clarification with unchanged existing timing semantics does not create material stability concern.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: none: the change is optional and additive for R4-to-R6. Any R6-to-R4 loss is limited to an explicit flag whose core timing information can still be present in R4 `start`/`end`.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No better less-breaking base design is apparent. Keeping only implicit start/end comparison would preserve the R4 model but would not meet the R6 goal of making counter-proposals directly computable.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: disagree: I agree that the field is optional and the alternative is Not applicable, but I would not classify the finding as Medium impact because there is no meaningful R4-to-R6 compatibility problem.

findings.title: recurrence-specific response fields added

oldState.summary: R4 had no local recurrence fields on AppointmentResponse.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could respond to an Appointment, but did not have native fields to say that one response applies to all occurrences or to identify a specific occurrence in a recurring request.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 can indicate whether the response applies to all occurrences and can identify a specific recurring occurrence by date or recurrence sequence.

semanticText.short: This response is for all occurrences in a recurring request / Original date within a recurring request / The recurrence ID of the specific recurring request
semanticText.definition: `recurring` indicates that the AppointmentResponse applies to all occurrences in a recurring request; `occurrenceDate` is the original date within a recurring request; `recurrenceId` is the sequence number of the specific appointment when responding to a recurring request.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: These three R6 elements have no R4 element ids and form a coherent recurrence-response addition.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The fields are optional, so R4 data can migrate to R6 without validation failure. R6→R4 conversion is high risk when these fields are populated because R4 lacks native representation for whether a response applies to all occurrences or to a specific occurrence. Dropping the fields can change scheduling scope.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Applying a participant response to the wrong occurrence or to an entire series can cause missed, duplicated, or incorrectly accepted/declined appointments.

justification.inferredGoal: Support recurring appointment workflows in the base scheduling model.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the recurrence fields are optional R6 additions and do not invalidate existing R4 AppointmentResponse instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of supporting recurring appointment workflows in the base scheduling model is reasonable, and adding optional fields is a proportionate base design because it preserves R4-to-R6 structural compatibility. The serious risk is down-conversion: dropping recurrence scope can change whether a response applies to one occurrence or an entire series.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: An extension-only approach would help R4 backports but would leave recurrence behavior profile-specific and less visible to generic R6 scheduling clients. Because the R6 additions are optional and preserve R4 instances, the backward-compatible-alternative question is `Not applicable` rather than `No`.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Native recurrence fields create lossy R6-to-R4 cases when populated, but they do not require changing R4-valid data during R4-to-R6 migration.

evidence.detail: R4 has no `recurring`, `occurrenceDate`, or `recurrenceId` elements on AppointmentResponse.
R6 adds optional boolean `recurring`.
evidence.quote: Indicates that this AppointmentResponse applies to all occurrences in a recurring request.

evidence.detail: R6 adds optional date `occurrenceDate`.
evidence.quote: The original date within a recurring request.

evidence.detail: R6 adds optional positiveInt `recurrenceId`.
evidence.quote: The recurrence ID (sequence number) of the specific appointment when responding to a recurring request.

evidence.detail: R6 Appointment includes recurrence-related fields, confirming that the response fields are part of a broader recurring scheduling model.

examples.examplesMd: R4 can reference an Appointment and carry the status, but it cannot natively preserve the fact that this decline applies only to occurrence 3 on 2026-07-08.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds a set of recurrence fields to `AppointmentResponse`. They are not required, but when present they materially affect the scope of the response.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: There is no R4→R6 validation break because the new elements are optional. R6 instances using them are not losslessly representable in R4, and a naive converter that drops the fields can turn a per-occurrence response into an ambiguous response to the series or template appointment.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4→R6, populate recurrence fields only when the source system has reliable recurrence metadata. For R6→R4, preserve recurrence scope in extensions or split/route responses according to implementation policy; do not silently discard `recurring`, `occurrenceDate`, or `recurrenceId` in scheduling workflows.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The native additions are justified for recurring scheduling interoperability. A pure extension approach would have been less disruptive for R4 but would not give base R6 clients computable recurrence semantics.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The recurrence fields are optional additions, so they do not reject R4 AppointmentResponse instances. They do, however, introduce meaningful R6-to-R4 loss when populated: dropping whether a response applies to all occurrences, a specific date, or a recurrence sequence can change scheduling scope. The native R6 design is proportionate because recurring appointment support needs computable base fields and the additions preserve R4-to-R6 structural compatibility.
keyEvidence: R6 adds optional `recurring` 0..1 boolean, `occurrenceDate` 0..1 date, and `recurrenceId` 0..1 positiveInt.
R6 definitions describe all-series responses, original occurrence dates, and recurrence sequence numbers for recurring appointment requests.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 3/trial-use raises concern for recurring scheduling workflows, but the changes are additive and targeted to a legitimate base-model gap.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: R4-valid data remains valid in R6, but populated R6 recurrence fields cannot be losslessly represented in base R4 and losing them can alter per-occurrence versus whole-series response meaning.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No superior less-breaking R6 base design is evident. Leaving recurrence only to extensions or profiles would be easier for R4 backports but would not provide generic R6 clients with computable recurrence scope; the optional native fields preserve R4 instances while addressing the new workflow.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree: the existing report's High R6-to-R4 representability concern and Not applicable alternative assessment are consistent with the fresh path-level review, though the change remains proportionate.

facts.newValue: v3 _ParticipationAncillary descendants; v3 LOC descendants; participant-type

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element and binding canonical are unchanged, but the value set compose changed. Full expansion comparison was not possible from the supplied R6 core package alone.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The binding remains extensible, so this is not a direct hard validation break like a required binding removal. It can still affect conformance, terminology validation warnings, auto-complete lists, and matching logic because some R4-preferred codes may no longer be in the R6 preferred set and R6 adds location-role coverage not present in R4's compose.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Participant role coding is used to match AppointmentResponse participants to Appointment participants; changed preferred terminology can affect automated matching.

justification.inferredGoal: Refine preferred participant-role terminology, especially location roles.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the R4 explicit `SPRF`, `PPRF`, and `PART` includes while adding the R6 `LOC` hierarchy and `ELOC` exclusion.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding location-role coverage is a reasonable goal, but the local evidence does not show that the old explicit `SPRF`, `PPRF`, and `PART` includes had to be dropped to achieve it. Because the binding remains extensible, the current change is not a hard validation break, yet it can still affect terminology validation, auto-complete, and participant matching. The supplied compose definitions show a straightforward less-breaking value-set design, so the disruptive part is not clearly justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking R6 base value set could include the old explicit R4 concepts and add the new `LOC` descendant filter while retaining the R6 `ELOC` exclusion. That would preserve R4-preferred participant-role codes for systems that already use them and still add the new location-role coverage. The tradeoff is a less curated and possibly broader preferred value set; if HL7 intentionally de-preferred the old performer or generic participation concepts, official rationale or expansion notes would be needed to justify that choice.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: A broader preferred set may retain role codes R6 wanted to discourage, but it avoids removing R4-preferred concepts and does not create duplicate fields or validation ambiguity beyond ordinary extensible-binding breadth.

evidence.detail: R4 binding is extensible to ValueSet/encounter-participant-type.
R4 compose includes v3 _ParticipationAncillary descendants, explicit SPRF/PPRF/PART, and participant-type; excludes _ParticipationAncillary.
R6 binding remains extensible to ValueSet/encounter-participant-type.
R6 compose includes v3 _ParticipationAncillary descendants, v3 LOC descendants, and participant-type; excludes _ParticipationAncillary and ELOC.

examples.examplesMd: The example illustrates a code explicitly included by the R4 compose but not explicitly included by the R6 compose. Because the binding is extensible and no authoritative expansions were available, this should be treated as a conformance-risk example rather than a proven hard invalid instance.

findings.narrativeMd: `AppointmentResponse.participantType` keeps the same extensible binding canonical, but the underlying value set composition changes. This matters for systems that validate, suggest, or compare participant roles based on the bound value set rather than accepting arbitrary CodeableConcepts.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: The binding strength remains extensible, so ordinary structural validation should not fail solely because a coding is outside the value set. However, terminology validation can change warnings or conformance decisions. R6 values using the newly included `LOC` hierarchy may not be preferred in R4, and R4 values using explicit `PPRF`, `SPRF`, or `PART` need expansion-based review in R6.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not hard-code the R4 participantType expansion for R6. Refresh terminology services and matching tables, and test role matching between Appointment.participant.type and AppointmentResponse.participantType using local production codes. If `PPRF`, `SPRF`, or `PART` appear in source data, review whether R6 prefers a more specific replacement or permits the old coding as an additional coding/text.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change may have been made to refine role semantics, but the supplied inputs do not show why old explicit includes were dropped. A backward-compatible alternative would keep old includes while adding the new location hierarchy, at the cost of a larger and possibly less curated value set.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Requires a terminology-service expansion using the exact R4 and R6 terminology package versions before classifying any specific participantType code as removed or added with high confidence.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `participantType` keeps an extensible binding to the same value-set canonical, but the compose changes: R6 adds location-role coverage and no longer explicitly includes R4's `SPRF`, `PPRF`, and `PART` concepts. Because the binding is extensible, this is not a hard validation break, but it can affect terminology warnings, value-set-driven pick lists, and role matching for a path used to align AppointmentResponse participants with Appointment participants. The local evidence shows a plausible low-cost base alternative: retain the R4 explicit includes while adding the R6 location hierarchy and exclusion.
keyEvidence: R4 `AppointmentResponse.participantType` is 0..* CodeableConcept with extensible binding to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/encounter-participant-type`.

R4 `ValueSet-encounter-participant-type` compose includes v3 `_ParticipationAncillary` descendants, explicit v3 `SPRF`, `PPRF`, and `PART`, and `participant-type`, excluding `_ParticipationAncillary`.

R6 keeps the same extensible binding canonical but compose includes v3 `_ParticipationAncillary` descendants, v3 `LOC` descendants, and `participant-type`, excluding `_ParticipationAncillary` and `ELOC`.
The local v3 ParticipationType CodeSystem shows `LOC`/`ELOC` and `PPRF`/`SPRF` as distinct concepts; full R6 expansion evidence was not available in the core package.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 3/trial-use means warning-level terminology churn does not automatically warrant redesign, but this is mature enough that unexplained de-preference of existing role concepts on a participant-matching path deserves attention when a modest compatibility-preserving compose exists.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: warning-level: the extensible binding prevents an old-valid/new-invalid hard break, but terminology validation, auto-complete, and code-based participant matching can change when R4-preferred concepts are no longer in the preferred compose.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could keep the R4 explicit `SPRF`, `PPRF`, and `PART` includes while adding the `LOC` hierarchy and `ELOC` exclusion. The tradeoff is a broader, less curated preferred value set if R6 intentionally wanted to discourage those concepts, but the supplied evidence does not show that this tradeoff was necessary.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree: the existing report's Yes alternative judgment is supported, and the impact is best understood as warning-level/conformance rather than hard break; that still justifies Revisit because the less-breaking base design is straightforward.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The same canonical `http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/AppointmentResponse`, id, type, resource kind, base `DomainResource`, derivation, and abstract=false flag are present in R4 and R6. No rename, split, merge, or removal was found.
All R4 local elements remain present in R6. R6 adds optional local elements documented in findings; no local R4 element was removed or renamed.

Existing local element cardinalities are unchanged: `appointment` and `participantStatus` remain 1..1; `identifier`, `start`, `end`, `participantType`, `actor`, and `comment` retain their R4 min/max values. New elements are optional.

Existing local element types are unchanged except `comment`, which is covered as a finding. No choice element type additions/removals were found because AppointmentResponse has no local choice elements.
`appointment` still targets `Appointment`. `actor` adds `Group`, which is covered as a finding; no target was removed.
Binding strength did not increase for local elements. Material value-set changes for `participantStatus` and `participantType` are covered as findings.

The local invariant `apr-1` remains an error with the same expression `participantType.exists() or actor.exists()`. R6 adds `condition: ["apr-1"]` annotations on the affected elements, but this points to the existing invariant rather than adding a new validation rule. Inherited `dom-*` and `ele-1` details are out of scope.
No fixed value, pattern value, or default value constraints were found on local AppointmentResponse elements in either version.

No local minValue, maxValue, maxLength, or regex constraint was added to an AppointmentResponse element. Primitive-level string/markdown details are considered through the `comment` type finding and base primitive reports.

No local modifier flag toggled. `participantStatus` remains a modifier; its reason and required terminology changed and are covered in the status finding. Inherited modifierExtension behavior is out of scope.
Existing local summary flags are unchanged. The added `proposedNewTime` element is summary=true and is covered in its finding; recurrence additions are summary=false.
No local slicing definitions or slice identity changes were found.

No element name or choice-suffix serialization change was found for existing local elements. R6-only elements and the `comment` primitive-type change create serialization/codegen considerations documented in findings.

R6-to-R4 representability issues were identified for `participantStatus=entered-in-error`, `actor=Group`, `proposedNewTime`, and recurrence fields. No additional local representability issue was found beyond the findings.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Artifact maturity/status metadata advanced
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The canonical identity and structural kind did not change. R6 changes metadata from draft/trial-use to active/normative, which affects governance expectations but not instance shape.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Policy, documentation, and conformance claims may need updating because implementations may treat normative artifacts differently from trial-use artifacts.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 annotates participantType and actor as affected by apr-1
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The actual `apr-1` invariant expression and severity remain unchanged. The new `condition` metadata improves traceability but does not add a new validation rule.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Code generators or documentation renderers may now show the existing invariant next to the two affected elements.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Workflow and mapping metadata changed
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Mapping entries are not part of instance validation. R6 removes or revises some R4 workflow mapping metadata while retaining the clinical data elements.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Tools that derive transforms from StructureDefinition `mapping` entries should compare mappings directly instead of assuming the R4 workflow mappings still exist in R6.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: `AppointmentResponse.proposedNewTime`, recurrence fields, `actor`, and `participantType` are interpreted relative to the referenced `Appointment`. The companion Appointment report should own structural changes to Appointment itself.
A terminology-service expansion is needed to confirm exact added/removed participant role concepts across R4 and R6 terminology package versions.
Inherited contained-resource, narrative, extension, and modifierExtension changes appear in the snapshots but are intentionally excluded from this local AppointmentResponse report.
